content: 1. Topiramate may reduce the levels or effects of conjugated estrogens (vaginal) by influencing the metabolism of hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Close monitoring is advised when these medications are used together. 2. Trazodone may decrease the levels or effects of conjugated estrogens (vaginal) through the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. The interaction mechanism is unspecified, and the clinical significance is unknown. Estrogens and progestins may reduce the effects of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) while increasing TCA plasma concentrations and associated adverse effects. 3. Verapamil may increase the levels or effects of conjugated estrogens (vaginal) by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism and through the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Close monitoring is recommended. 4. Voriconazole may increase the levels or effects of conjugated estrogens (vaginal) by influencing hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 5. Zafirlukast may increase the levels or effects of conjugated estrogens (vaginal) by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 6. Common adverse effects of conjugated estrogens include abdominal pain, dizziness, breast enlargement, and urinary urgency. Genitourinary side effects may include abnormal uterine bleeding or spotting, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, increased uterine leiomyoma size, vaginitis (including vaginal candidiasis), changes in cervical secretions, cystitis-like syndrome, vulvovaginal discomfort (burning, irritation, genital pruritus), endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial cancer, precocious puberty, and leukorrhea. 7. Breast-related side effects include tenderness, enlargement, pain, discharge, fibrocystic breast changes, breast cancer, and gynecomastia in males. 8. Cardiovascular risks include deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and increased blood pressure. 9. Gastrointestinal side effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, bloating, and an increased incidence of gallbladder disease. 10. Dermatological effects include chloasma (which may persist after discontinuation), scalp hair loss, hirsutism, and rash. 11. Ocular side effects include retinal vascular thrombosis and intolerance to contact lenses. 12. Central nervous system effects include headache, migraine, dizziness, mental depression, nervousness, mood disturbances, irritability, and dementia. 13. Miscellaneous effects include weight changes, glucose intolerance, edema, arthralgias, leg cramps, libido changes, urticaria, asthma exacerbation, increased triglycerides, and hypersensitivity reactions. 14. Conjugated estrogens are contraindicated in cases of undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, known or suspected breast cancer, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, active or history of DVT, PE, arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, MI), anaphylactic reaction or angioedema to estrogen preparations, liver dysfunction or disease, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiency, known thrombophilic disorders, and known or suspected pregnancy. 15. Systemic absorption occurs with the use of vaginal cream. Adding a progestin for 10 or more days of an estrogen cycle or daily in a continuous regimen may reduce the incidence of endometrial hyperplasia compared to estrogen alone. Endometrial hyperplasia may be a precursor to endometrial cancer. 16. Progestin use with estrogens may increase the risk of breast cancer compared to estrogen-alone regimens. Estrogens should be discontinued at least 4-6 weeks before surgery associated with increased thromboembolism risk or during prolonged immobilization. 17. Most studies show no significant increased risk of endometrial cancer with estrogen use for less than one year. Prolonged use (5-10 years or more) is associated with a 15to 24-fold increased risk, which may persist for 8-15 years after discontinuation. 18. Women should receive annual breast examinations by a healthcare provider, perform monthly breast self-examinations, and schedule mammography based on age, risk factors, and prior results. 19. Estrogens increase the risk of gallbladder disease. Severe hypercalcemia or hypertriglyceridemia warrants discontinuation of estrogen therapy. 20. Thyroid function should be monitored in women on thyroid replacement therapy. Estrogens may be poorly metabolized in women with impaired liver function. Caution is advised in women with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with estrogen use or pregnancy; recurrence warrants discontinuation. 21. Hormonal therapy for menopausal symptoms is associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer. The duration of therapy associated with this risk is unknown. 22. Retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogens. Discontinue therapy if sudden partial or complete vision loss, proptosis, diplopia, or migraine occurs. If examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions, estrogens should be permanently discontinued. 23. Estrogens may cause fluid retention. Women with conditions influenced by fluid retention, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction, require careful observation when prescribed estrogen-alone therapy. 24. Rare cases of malignant transformation of residual endometrial implants have been reported in women treated post-hysterectomy with estrogen-alone therapy. For women with residual endometriosis post-hysterectomy, adding a progestin should be considered. 25. Estrogen therapy should be used cautiously in women with hypoparathyroidism, as estrogen-induced hypocalcemia may occur. 26. Rare cases of anaphylaxis and angioedema have been reported. Estrogens may exacerbate symptoms of hereditary angioedema. 27. Estrogens may worsen asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraine, porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas. 28. Premarin cream may weaken latex condoms, diaphragms, or cervical caps, potentially contributing to their failure. 29. Estrogens are classified as Pregnancy Category X and are contraindicated during pregnancy. They are distributed in human breast milk and may reduce milk quantity and quality. Caution is advised during breastfeeding. 30. Estradiol is largely bound to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin, widely distributed throughout the body, with higher concentrations in sex hormone target organs. Estradiol is reversibly converted to estrone, and both can be converted to estriol, a major urinary metabolite. Estrogens undergo enterohepatic recirculation via sulfate and glucuronide conjugation in the liver, biliary secretion into the intestine, hydrolysis in the intestine, and reabsorption. 31. Estradiol, estrone, and estriol are excreted in the urine along with glucuronide and sulfate conjugates.
